lessonRef.title: Concept model B: building and reading two-way frequency tables

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Compare these two examples. Find the step where they stop being the same.

items.prompt: Group X: 12 successes, 8 failures. Find P(success | X).
P(A) = 5/10, P(B) = 4/10, P(A and B) = 20/100. Independent?

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Work these with your teaching parent. Say the reason for each step out loud before you write it.

items.prompt: In a group of 33, 16 do activity A, 19 do activity B, and 10 do both. Find P(A or B) as a fraction in lowest terms.
An event has probability 4/5 on a single trial. Two independent trials are run. Find the probability of at least one success, as a fraction in lowest terms.
A survey table records: group X with 14 successes and 16 failures; group Y with 18 successes and 7 failures. Find P(success | group X) as a fraction in lowest terms.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: Two events have P(A) = 8/10, P(B) = 3/10, and P(A and B) = 27/100. Are A and B independent?
choices: No; P(A and B) differs from P(A)·P(B).
Yes; the two events cannot occur together.
Yes; P(A and B) equals P(A)·P(B).
No; the two events are mutually exclusive.

items.prompt: In a group of 29, 15 do activity A, 9 do activity B, and 4 do both. Find P(A or B) as a fraction in lowest terms.
An event has probability 5/6 on a single trial. Two independent trials are run. Find the probability of at least one success, as a fraction in lowest terms.
A survey table records: group X with 28 successes and 23 failures; group Y with 27 successes and 31 failures. Find P(success | group X) as a fraction in lowest terms.
